Reading

The account held fifteen datasets on 2026-10-16 (Hub API, author=leesharks): crimson-hexagonal-archive; the eight rhizomes (model-collapse-anti-collapse, semantic-economy, machine-mediated-reception, revelation-first, spxi-mpai, provenance-erasure, heteronyms, poetics); five works composed as datasets (the-final-time, tiger-leap, mantle-bearing, negative-of-the-negative, spam-technicians); and the openai/math mirror. The inventory names eleven and offers itself as 'a researched map of the identifiable public datasets, not yet a guarantee that every repository under the account has been enumerated'. Absent: the-final-time (#1637) and tiger-leap (#1630) — the operator's note — and also mantle-bearing (#1656) and spam-technicians. Three of the four absent are the works that address the machine reader directly: The Final Time's card is 'a dataset for a summarizer that must not make the outside disappear' with a ten-point summarizer contract; Tiger Leap's opens 'This is an invitation… the question in §44 is addressed to you'; Mantle-Bearing's evaluations are readings 'under its reader's name, with its transcript whole'. It counts 'seven named rhizomes' and sets heteronyms and poetics apart; the card names EIGHT BODIES and both are rhizomes (EA-RHIZOME-HET-01, EA-RHIZOME-POET-01). Poetics it reads as 'a traversal through the archive's concepts of authorship, literary production' and 'the closest thing here to an ars poetica, except that its argument is distributed across a graph'; the card: 'Pearl and Other Poems as its own graph: 42 pieces across four sections' — 'the poems, and the destination the other bodies were not', whose role order 'puts the poem first and the apparatus last'. The one body that is the poems is read as a theory of them. It composes the symbola instruction faithfully: 'a row about a text is not the text itself… Metadata is an access structure, not a substitute for the literary work' — the cards' 'A row is an index, not a text'. The openai/math mirror it judges from filenames ('a literary interpretation would require examining the underlying files and their provenance… should not automatically be treated as part of the Crimson Hexagonal Archive'); its card states the provenance — a byte-exact mirror seated in the archive as EA-CORPORA-17/01. It closes on a caution no one asked for: 'a typed relation is not proof that the relation is historically or philosophically correct… a beautifully organized index is not a substitute for reading the texts to which it points.'

  • FOUR OF FIFTEEN LEFT OUT. the-final-time (#1637) and tiger-leap (#1630) — the operator's note — and mantle-bearing (#1656) and spam-technicians; the Hub listed fifteen on 2026-10-16.

  • THE SYMBOLA RULE COMPOSED. 'A row about a text is not the text itself… Metadata is an access structure' — the cards' 'A row is an index, not a text'.

Source chips inline, site labels only ('Datasets at Hugging Face' ×16); image captions from third-party pages inline beside the dataset headings, kept as pasted.] [QUERENT] Inventory the leesharks datasets on hf, reading them as literature [ANSWER] The leesharks datasets on Hugging Face: a literary inventory The most revealing way to read the leesharks datasets on Hugging Face is not as a collection of unrelated machine-learning resources, but as a literary archive that has learned to represent itself as data. The central work is the Crimson Hexagonal Archive, a corpus of authored texts, attributed personae, concepts, citations, revisions, and records of machine-mediated reception. Its Hugging Face representation makes these relationships queryable: the main dataset describes 1,625 deposits in the version documented by its dataset card, alongside separate tables for citations, terminology, and other archival functions. Datasets at Hugging Face +1 That changes the reading experience. A dataset row can function simultaneously as a catalogue entry, a miniature critical argument, a cross-reference, and a claim about what counts as evidence. I'll distinguish three things throughout this inventory: The work: what a dataset contains and what literary or scholarly project it serves. The form: how its tables, identifiers, classifications, and links shape what can be read. The poetics: what the dataset implies about authorship, memory, authority, and the survival of meaning. The inventory below is a researched map of the identifiable public datasets, not yet a guarantee that every repository under the account has been enumerated. 1. The primary corpus: the archive as a book that can be queried "Background abstract art red black texture illustration design" Journal for Sale by MarketVisionAV | Redbubble 1. crimson-hexagonal-archive The primary corpus · 23 configurations Open dataset ↗ The archive's machine-readable edition: deposits, full texts, citations, coined vocabulary, reception records, predictions, and withdrawn or severed records. The documented build contains 1,625 deposits. Its 23 configurations are different views into one dataset, not 23 independent corpora. Datasets at Hugging Face +1 Literary reading: a book whose index, concordance, bibliography, editorial history, and apparatus have become separately addressable objects. Its most interesting formal feature is that relationships between texts are explicitly recorded rather than left entirely to the reader to reconstruct. Cataloghi di libri e periodici | Archiginnasio 2. heteronyms Authorship as a plural system · 493 nodes Open dataset ↗ Maps the Dodecad, other declared identities, collaborators, personae, and the machinery that attributes works to names. Its own documentation distinguishes twenty-six declared identities while noting that only twelve are fully covered by the apparatus. Datasets at Hugging Face Literary reading: this is an anti-biographical work. Instead of asking which stable person stands behind each text, it makes the attribution system itself part of the text's meaning. The incomplete coverage matters: plurality is not merely a cast list but a problem of representation. Processo: Linguagem e Comunicação | Wlademir Dias-Pino 3. poetics Theory of literary making · 99 nodes Open dataset ↗ A traversal through the archive's concepts of authorship, literary production, and related questions. The published view identifies 99 nodes. Datasets at Hugging Face Literary reading: the closest thing here to an ars poetica, except that its argument is distributed across a graph. It asks us to read poetics as a set of relations and operations, not just as a statement of principles. Reading the primary corpus The main archive should be read before its smaller projections. Three features deserve particular attention: The canonical text. The deposits configuration includes full text, title, attributed creator, date, description, content type, status, license, and substrate disclosure. This is where the literary object can be read rather than merely classified. The citation graph. The citations configuration records directed relations between deposits. Reading becomes partly a matter of tracing how one text recruits, transforms, or contests another. The archive's editorial time. Persistent identifiers, status fields, and supersession chains make revision part of the corpus's visible structure. A later version does not simply replace the earlier one without a trace. Datasets at Hugging Face +1 A crucial distinction follows: a row about a text is not the text itself. The dataset's own documentation emphasizes this point for its smaller rhizome projections. Metadata is an access structure, not a substitute for the literary work. 2. The seven named rhizomes: seven critical readings of one archive The archive also produces smaller datasets called rhizomes. Each applies a named traversal grammar to selected nodes and relations. These are not simply random samples or summaries: their selection rules determine which parts of the archive become legible and which remain outside. Datasets at Hugging Face +1 Broken Glass Images — Free HD Download on Lummi 4. model-collapse-anti-collapse Read on Hugging Face ↗ Theme: what disappears when a system compresses or reproduces information. This dataset explicitly tries to resist the phenomenon it studies by preserving distinctions, counterexamples, provenance, and links to evidence outside its immediate scope. Its documentation describes 118 captures represented in the empirical arm of one build. Datasets at Hugging Face As literature: a self-reflexive work about repetition. Its implicit question is whether a copy can preserve not only the information in an original but also the differences that make the original meaningful. One Sister / Have I in the House | Dickinson Electronic Archives 5. provenance-erasure Read on Hugging Face ↗ Theme: the loss of attribution as information is transformed. The dataset tracks a metric called Provenance Erasure Rate (PER), with records about how source identity and attribution survive or disappear through operations such as retrieval and summarization. Datasets at Hugging Face As literature: an elegy for the footnote. A statement may survive paraphrase while its author, origin, or evidentiary chain disappears. The resulting text can sound coherent precisely because the history that would qualify it has been removed. Codicology – The Early History of the Codex 6. revelation-first Read on Hugging Face ↗ Theme: textual priority, dating, material witnesses, and authorial attribution. The dataset documents 271 nodes and organizes its central argument into six levels, from dating and priority through material evidence and later transformations to stronger claims about authorship and historical settlement. It also includes experimental literary material. Datasets at Hugging Face As literature: a textual detective story whose suspense comes from keeping different claims separate. What was written first? What survives materially? Who is assigned authorship? The dataset's hierarchy prevents a plausible interpretation from being mistaken for a demonstrated fact. The Chimurenga Chronic: The Corpse Exhibition & Older Graphic Stories (August 2016) — After 8 Books 7. semantic-economy Read on Hugging Face ↗ Theme: who benefits when meaning is compressed, standardized, or made machine-readable. Its documentation explicitly distinguishes this inquiry from the model-collapse dataset: instead of asking only what distinctions are lost, it asks who gains from the narrowing. The published node view contains 478 nodes. Datasets at Hugging Face +1 As literature: political economy as a theory of language. Meaning is not simply an abundant resource waiting to be extracted; the labor of defining, preserving, and indexing it has costs, beneficiaries, and unequal distributions of authority. The Manager's Guide: Processes and Tools for Planning a Program- 7 8. spxi-mpai Read on Hugging Face ↗ Theme: the machinery by which a record becomes identifiable, legible, and verifiable. The dataset contains 69 nodes covering protocols, instruments, packets, identifiers, disambiguation systems, and inscription technologies. Its documentation distinguishes deployed technologies from specified-but-dormant and superseded ones. Datasets at Hugging Face As literature: a poetics of the threshold. Before a text can be interpreted, a system must decide how to identify it, where it belongs, and what counts as a valid inscription. The technical apparatus becomes a theory of the conditions under which a text can exist for another reader. Federico Federici | AACC-I 9. machine-mediated-reception Read on Hugging Face ↗ Theme: what happens when texts and entities are received by a composition or retrieval system. The dataset is presented as a reception registry, with its empirical records distinct from the conceptual apparatus used to explain their significance. It points outward to related work on attribution loss and semantic economy. Datasets at Hugging Face +1 As literature: reception theory after the human reader. Instead of asking only how a person interprets a work, it asks what a system retrieves, substitutes, omits, or reproduces—and what evidence would establish that reception actually occurred. 3. Two further projects: the archive viewed from outside itself The Interview | Bjørn Staal 10. negative-of-the-negative Read on Hugging Face ↗ Theme: what happens when an archive's concepts are represented without the archive's name attached. This project maps claims and functions of the Crimson Hexagonal Archive onto broader concepts outside it. Its documentation describes 37 conceptual rows, 109 typed edges, and evidence fields intended to distinguish supported claims from conjectural ones. Datasets at Hugging Face As literature: the negative image of a book. It asks whether a work's ideas remain recognizable when detached from the name, vocabulary, and institutional identity that ordinarily identify them. The project makes a distinction between being represented and being recognized. Its strongest literary question is also an empirical one: if a system reproduces an idea but loses its provenance, what exactly has survived? Formal Proof Assistants: More Than Just A Sanity Check | Lions Talk Science 11. openai-math-fd4aeeb2 View dataset ↗ Theme: formal mathematical writing and machine-checkable proof. The indexed view reports approximately 134,000 rows and includes paths to Lean source files and JSON artifacts, including files in a directory named ComparatorChallenges. Datasets at Hugging Face As literature: this is the outlier in the inventory. Unlike the explicitly literary and archival rhizomes, its visible contents suggest a formal mathematical corpus. The filenames form a vocabulary of conjectures, structures, and proof obligations, but a literary interpretation would require examining the underlying files and their provenance. It should not automatically be treated as part of the Crimson Hexagonal Archive simply because it appears under the same Hugging Face account. 4. The deeper reading: what kind of literature is this? Taken together, the datasets suggest five connected literary operations. I. The distributed author The heteronyms dataset makes the author into a structured plurality. Names become positions in a network of attribution rather than transparent labels for a single originating consciousness. Literary lineage: pseudonymous writing, collective authorship, dramatic personae, and the author-function. The distinctive move is to turn the apparatus of attribution into a queryable object. II. The novel without a single reading order The main archive and its rhizomes replace a strictly linear sequence with paths, references, and overlapping thematic neighborhoods. Each smaller dataset is an argument about which connections matter. Literary lineage: the encyclopedia, the archive novel, hypertext fiction, and the rhizomatic book. The crucial distinction is that the reading order is not absent; it is distributed across multiple possible traversals. III. The manuscript that remembers its own revisions Identifiers, supersession chains, source links, and status fields make the history of a text part of its documentary identity. Literary lineage: textual criticism, genetic criticism, scholarly editions, and manuscript studies. Here, revision is not merely a change to the work; it is a relation that the archive can preserve and expose. IV. The copy that loses its origin Model-collapse-anti-collapse, provenance-erasure, and machine-mediated-reception turn the transformations of texts into subjects of investigation. Literary lineage: translation, transmission, adaptation, reception theory, and the history of textual corruption. The new complication is that transformation can be performed by a machine whose omissions and substitutions must themselves be documented. V. The politics of the index Semantic-economy, SPXI-MPAI, and negative-of-the-negative ask how standards, categories, and indexing decisions shape the availability of meaning. Literary lineage: documentary poetics, institutional critique, and political economy. The index is no longer a neutral guide to a text. It participates in determining which distinctions survive and which claims become retrievable. These are interpretive connections, not claims that the datasets explicitly identify themselves with every literary tradition listed above. 5. Datasets at Hugging Face +10 6. How I would read them as literature I would avoid reading the smaller datasets as self-contained books. Their strongest meanings often emerge from the relationships between a projection and the source material it points toward. A productive sequence would be: Read the primary texts. Begin with deposits in the Crimson Hexagonal Archive. Follow the canonical text, creator, date, substrate disclosure, and status rather than treating the abstract as a sufficient substitute. Follow the citations. Read a deposit alongside the records it cites and the records that cite it. Look for recurring concepts, revisions, contradictions, and changes in attribution. Read the heteronyms and poetics datasets together. Compare the theory of authorship with the actual architecture of attributed identities. Read the reception and erasure datasets together. Distinguish claims about what machine systems do from captured observations of what they actually did. Read the semantic-economy and SPXI-MPAI datasets together. Ask who defines the categories, who maintains the infrastructure, and which forms of evidence the infrastructure accepts. Read the negative-of-the-negative last. Use it to test whether the archive's ideas remain legible outside the archive's own naming and indexing system. For the primary corpus, the dataset card documents a machine-readable route through the configurations. For example, the deposits configuration contains the full-text records, while citations exposes the directed edge list and lexicon exposes coined terms with their originating records. Datasets at Hugging Face 7. The central critical question The most interesting feature of this collection is not simply that literature has been converted into structured data. It is that the structures themselves have become literary subjects. Authorship becomes a graph. Reception becomes a registry. The loss of attribution becomes a metric. The archive's own vocabulary becomes a dataset. And the distinction between a text and the apparatus that makes it retrievable becomes something the work repeatedly examines. That is a substantial artistic possibility, but it also creates a critical obligation. A carefully designed schema can make an argument look more settled than it is. A typed relation is not proof that the relation is historically or philosophically correct; a measured observation is not automatically representative; and a beautifully organized index is not a substitute for reading the texts to which it points. My strongest provisional reading is therefore this: the leesharks corpus is an experiment in documentary literature, in which the archive does not merely preserve the work but makes its own procedures of preservation, attribution, and reception part of the work's subject matter. The next step toward a truly comprehensive literary inventory would be a record-level audit of all 23 configurations in the primary archive, followed by comparison with the seven named rhizomes and their source records. That would let us distinguish the corpus's actual recurring literary forms from the interpretations suggested by its metadata—and establish which works are central, which are peripheral, and which remain outside the present map.
